needs: A layered or physical structure: memory as stacked layers from small and fast to large and slow.

brief.title: The memory hierarchy, layer by layer
brief.idea: A computer stacks memory in layers, from tiny fast registers to huge slow drives, and keeps the data it is using in the small fast layers near the processor.

beats.say: Memory in a computer is not one thing. It is a stack of layers, each bigger and slower than the one above.
beats.show: A narrow layer appears at the top and wider layers stack below it, forming a pyramid.

beats.say: At the top, inside the processor, are the registers: a few hundred bytes, read in under a nanosecond.
beats.show: The top layer is labelled registers, with its size and speed.

beats.say: Below them sit three caches. The first holds sixty four kilobytes and answers in about one nanosecond.
beats.show: A layer labelled L1 cache appears with 64 KB and 1 ns.

beats.say: The next two hold one megabyte and thirty two megabytes, and take four and twelve nanoseconds.
beats.show: Layers L2 and L3 appear below L1 with their sizes and times.

beats.say: Main memory holds sixteen gigabytes, but one read takes about a hundred nanoseconds, a hundred times slower than the first cache.
beats.show: A much wider layer labelled RAM appears with 16 GB and 100 ns.

beats.say: At the bottom, the drive holds a terabyte and takes about a hundred microseconds, a thousand times slower again.
beats.show: The widest layer, SSD, appears at the base with 1 TB and 100 µs.

beats.say: When the processor needs a value, it checks each layer from the top and stops at the first that has it.
beats.show: A marker drops from the registers through L1, L2 and L3, and finds the value in RAM.

beats.say: That value is copied up into the caches, so the next read takes one nanosecond instead of a hundred.
beats.show: The value travels back up, leaving a copy in L3, L2 and L1.

beats.say: Small and fast at the top, big and slow at the bottom, and what a program uses most stays near the top.
beats.show: The whole pyramid is shown with the processor at its tip and the copied value highlighted in L1.
